title: Efficient Human Pose Estimation Leveraging Advanced Techniques with MediaPipe

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'Table 1 summarizes the experimental data' and later says 'Key statistics include:' but no Table 1 or actual numerical statistics are provided anywhere in the paper. The results section is effectively empty despite promising quantitative results.

The paper claims 'a 20% increase in the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric compared to existing solutions' and 'a reduction in processing time by approximately 30%' but provides no baseline values, comparison models, datasets, or tables/figures supporting these numbers.
The text says 'Figure 3 demonstrates the application of the optimized MediaPipe framework in a real-time setting', but no Figure 3 is included in the paper.
An embedded image is labeled 'Figure 0', but the text only refers to Figures 1, 2, and 3. Figure numbering is inconsistent and Figure 0 is never referenced in the text.

The paper repeatedly claims 'sophisticated algorithmic enhancements and optimisations' and 'refined algorithms' to MediaPipe, but the methodology section only describes basic pixel mapping, an angle formula, and curl counter logic. No actual modifications to the MediaPipe framework, model architecture, training, or inference pipeline are described.

MediaPipe is described as offering 'robust, real-time, multi-person pose estimation capabilities'. MediaPipe Pose/BlazePose is a single-person pose estimation framework; multi-person use requires additional detection/tracking logic, so this is a false capability claim.

The paper uses IoU, defined as 'Area of Overlap / Area of Union', as a primary pose-estimation performance metric, but for human pose landmarks there are no segmentation masks or bounding boxes that would define such areas. Standard pose metrics such as PCK, OKS, or MPJPE would be appropriate instead.

The angle formula uses raw difference of two arctan2 values: angle = arctan2(c_y-b_y, c_x-b_x) - arctan2(a_y-b_y, a_x-b_x). Without taking an absolute value or wrapping to [0,180] degrees, the computed angle can be negative or outside the expected joint-angle range, causing the thresholds 'angle > 160' and 'angle < 30' to fail for valid poses.

The reference list contains clearly fabricated placeholder references: 'Developer, B., 2020', 'Innovator, C., 2021', 'Researcher, A., 2021', and 'Zhang, Y., et al., 2020, Optimizing mediapipe for real-time pose estimation on mobile devices, Journal of Mobile Computing'. These do not correspond to real scholarly works.

The OpenPose reference is cited as 'IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 32, 172–186' with year 2019. The journal volume 32 corresponds to 2010, not 2019; the bibliographic details are inconsistent with the actual publication.
Papandreou et al., 'Towards accurate multi-person pose estimation in the wild', is cited as 2018 CVPR, but the paper was presented at CVPR 2017. The reference year is wrong.

The paper claims systematic recording of walking, running, and dynamic movements in controlled and natural settings, but provides no dataset details, number of participants, ground-truth annotations, camera specifications, or training/evaluation protocols. This makes the experimental design non-reproducible.

The text says 'Feedback from test participants and system operators is integrated to assess user experience and responsiveness', but no participant information, questionnaire, feedback data, or qualitative results are reported.

The paper claims the modified framework 'exhibits superior capabilities when compared to previous models documented in the literature' under low light and partial occlusions, but no comparative experiments or literature-derived benchmarks are presented to support this superiority.

Several listed references, including Alam et al. (2022), Kim et al. (2023), Yurtsever and Eken (2022), and Pavllo et al. (2019), are never cited in the text, suggesting a mismatch between the reference list and the actual manuscript.
